The co-op booked it as an indemnity dive and Ilan let the booking stand. The alternative was
a member who had never seated a core going out to the cradle in his place. The co-op wanted
a splice in the pump vault before the shift turned, and he was the splice.

Quiej met him at the lock with the form. She read him the class of the dive with her thumb
on the line, the way she read everything.

"A cold soak may be cut to four hours on a co-op indemnity dive," she said. "The board holds
six for everybody else. The indemnity buys the other two and it buys them out of your lungs.
The indemnified lose the lining first. That is not gallery talk, it is the reason the clause
exists, and it is printed above the place where your name goes."

"Four hours," Ilan said.

"Four hours."

"Then four hours is what I have."

"Four hours is what the co-op has. What you have is a refusal, and I am obliged to tell you
that you have it."

He did not read the form. He had read indemnity paper all his working life and had filled
two of them out himself, and he knew what was in this one before she turned it round. The co-op pays. The co-op takes the procedure that hurt
you, entire, and afterwards the procedure is not discussed.

"Witness it," he said.

"I will witness it. That is the whole of what I do."

They soaked four hours.

The loop would not start against him, and he did not ask it twice.

He had no tolerance for it and had never had any. Splicers worked dry, hands in a hole and
lungs doing what lungs did, and the register had never been asked to certify anything about
him but his patience. The rig read him and refused, the way a machine refuses a thing it was
built to refuse, and he let it. Quiej stood on the deck with the form against her thigh and
wrote down the hour.

So he went down on the hard line instead, hood and hose, breathing gallery air six hours old
down a hose he could feel the pumps in. It is the slow way and it is the way a man with his
lungs is allowed to go.

"Line dive," Quiej said, writing. "No loop. Member declined the loop. Steward present."

"Say the hour on the form."

"The hour is on the form."

The throat is the inner door of the lock and it was built by people who had never met him.
He folded himself down and through it and went out into the brine.

Eleven metres. He had crossed them more times than the co-op's log showed and had never once
needed to look, because there was nothing out there to look at: four metres from the throat
his own glove stopped existing. So he counted. He kept the intakes on his right where their
pitch sat lowest, and he let the current off the exchangers carry him a little to the left
the way it always carried, and at the count he put his hand out and the cradle was there,
ringing faintly under his fingers as the shelf worked a long way overhead.

The seating was not where the paper put it.

He had told the board that, with the drawing in his hand, and the drawing had gone back into
the file with the co-op's number on it and the board had thanked him for his time. The
read-key seating sat two fingers off the drawing, lower, and turned out of true, which is
where a man building it in a hurry would have put it. That is what had happened, and it was
in nobody's file.

His hands found it. They went along the yoke, over the four bolts and the welt of the old
repair, in under the lip, and it was there, and he had it seated before he had finished
thinking about the order of it. That was the whole of his value to the co-op and he
knew it. A splicer is a pair of hands that have stopped needing to be told.

He checked it twice. The second check is the one that gets paid for.

Then he came back.

The throat runs on a cycle. The cycle belongs to the co-op, it is set at the board two
hundred metres up the gallery, and a diver on the wire may ask for it to be held and may not
hold it himself. He asked. He was inside the hour they had given him and he asked anyway,
out of habit. The wire said nothing back, and the cycle came.

He had his shoulders through it and his hips through it and his left hand still out in the
water when the door began to close.

The throat releases from the vault side and from nowhere else. There is one release and it
is out in the brine, behind a man who is already through, because the co-op that built the
lock decided that the person who most needed the door held was the person still in the
water. Quiej was on the deck. There was nothing on the deck to pull.

He got his arm back.

He did not get the hand.

It took six hours to come up and none of it could be hurried. The lock climbs at the
rate a body will take and the body is not consulted. He lay on the deck with his wrist in a
clamp and the thinness behind his breastbone settling in to stay, and for four of those hours
Quiej did not speak, which he was grateful for, and for the last two she filled in the form.

"The co-op wants the read-key seating logged as completed," she said.

"It is completed."

"I know that it is. I am asking whether you want it in your name."

"Put it in my name."

She held the form where he could reach it. She did not look at the clamp and she did not look
away from it either. The line was at the bottom, under the clause that said what the co-op
takes and for how long, and he put the pen in his right hand and signed.

He did not say yes. She did not ask him to. That was the difference, and it was the only
thing he brought up out of the water that the form had no line for.
